newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN bars 20 Rwandans from asylum for genocide role.
newsitem.headline: UN bars 20 Rwandans from asylum for genocide role.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency said on Tuesday it was excluding from refugee status 20 Rwandans indicted by an international tribunal for crimes against civilians during the mass ethnic killings of 1994.
In an usually bold public statement, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) urged states to "take the same measure" if the named Rwandans sought asylum in their countries.

The UNHCR, twice winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, said it only barred people from international protection as a refugee if they were strongly suspected of having committed "a crime against peace, a war crime or a crime against humanity".
"The 20 Rwandans are believed to be among those behind the execution and planning of the genocide in which more than 500,000 Rwandans were killed," the statement said.
Most of the 20 are "known to be in Europe and Africa", according to the Geneva-based UNHCR.
The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, based in Arusha, Tanzania, has indicted all 20 named suspects, including eight who are in custody there.
Three await trial soon by the same tribunal after being arraigned last June on charges of having taken part in the ethnic slaughter by hardline Hutus.

The three, detained in Zambia last year and extradited to Arusha in May, are Georges Rutaganda, an agricultural engineer and alleged former vice president of the Interahamwe militia, Jean Paul Akayesu, a senior local official of Taba commune and Clement Kayishema, former prefect of Kibuye province.
Rutaganda faces eight counts and is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and by drowning.
Akayesu faces 12 counts of ordering killings of civilians, including five secondary school teachers.
Another of the 20 indicted, Obeid Ruzindana, was arrested in Kenya on Friday, according to state radio.
The arrest of Ruzindana, an exiled Rwandan Hutu businessman, was the first by Kenya, seen by Rwanda's new Tutsi-led government as a haven for Hutus who fled after the genocide.

It was not clear how many of the named suspects were among 1.7 million Rwandans staying in refugee camps in neighbouring Zaire and Tanzania, run by the UNHCR. "There must be some in Zaire, too," a spokeswoman told a news briefing.
UNHCR oversees the 1951 U.N. Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, signed by 131 countries, which defines refugees' basic rights and sets minimum standards of treatment.
The pact contains a clause providing for exclusion of any person suspected to have committed a "crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity".
The 1969 refugee convention of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), contains a similar exclusion clause, UNHCR said.
Ruth Marshall, UNHCR spokeswoman, told Reuters: "We've used the technique of exclusion in the past, but it has not usually been public.

"We've excluded Afghans, Iranians and Iraqis who have worked for the secret services in their countries, any number of drug dealers as well as people who participated in death squads in their countries, for example in El Salvador," she added.
